reasons: The claim and action are supported: the excerpt says bundles can pass shipping/fulfillment efficiency to customers while increasing units per transaction, a major AOV lever.

The declared dependency is not supported and creates a circular structure with candidate 26e95…: the excerpt presents bundling as useful in its own right and does not require a bundle to have a shipping-savings-funded discount.
The principle accurately reflects the excerpt's stated rationale that free shipping is not always beneficial and that collected shipping is almost pure profit for most people.
The candidate preserves the source's qualifier 'for most people' in its unknowns.
The recommended use of a free-shipping threshold to incentivize higher orders, and the need to test threshold placement, are supported by the excerpt.

The dependency on candidate 98e145… is not established as a prerequisite in the excerpt. The source discusses free-shipping trade-offs, but does not say that adopting the stated principle must precede threshold testing.

The candidate correctly identifies that the excerpt uses both 'about 10% of the average order value of the cart' and 'sub 10% of total revenue,' and correctly notes that the asserted conversion impact lacks defined measurement and test details.
Its dependency on candidate 98e145… is not stated in the excerpt; the numerical shipping-charge assertion is presented directly, not as depending on first adopting that principle.
The excerpt supports presenting a one-click upsell immediately after purchase without re-entering card details.
It explicitly qualifies that the upsell must be relevant to the item just purchased rather than a random add-on, which the candidate retains.
The ritual-bag price, reference-price framing, and five-minute post-checkout example are accurately identified as an example rather than a universal requirement.
The excerpt explicitly characterizes the 20%-off offer as margin-eroding, lazy discounting that does not increase AOV, while saying revenue may rise and profit fall.
The candidate's warning is confined to the source's described blanket 20%-off framing.
The excerpt explicitly warns that repeated broad discounting trains customers to wait for discounts and can make a brand reliant on its 20%-off-everything reputation.
The candidate appropriately notes that the excerpt provides no recovery path or timeline.
The product composition, three-step framing, and stated $122 AOV are accurately presented as elements of the source's worked example.
The candidate does not present the illustrative $122 result as a general measured result, and notes the absence of store, period, and sample details.
The excerpt's example directly states that a $14 bundle discount takes a stated $136 value to $122 and is margin-neutral because separately shipping the three items would cost an additional $14.
The candidate retains the necessary condition that the claimed margin neutrality is contingent on the merchant actually having equivalent shipping and fulfillment savings.
The dependency on having a bundle is consistent with a discount applied across that bundle.

The claim and action are supported by the described example: a serum-only cart can be upgraded in one click to add the cleanser and recovery cream, with the framed benefits of savings, free shipping, and a gift.

The dependency on the worked routine-bundle example is supported, but the additional dependency target 'missing-local:u10' is unresolvable and unsupported by the supplied excerpt. It should be removed or replaced with a defined, source-grounded prerequisite.
The excerpt says reviews are the biggest trust signal, tells startups to prioritize them, and says nothing else in the chapter really matters when there are no reviews.
The candidate accurately preserves the source's two differently stated ranges: roughly doubling conversion from zero to 100 reviews and the largest jump occurring from zero to 80.
Its limitations correctly note that these conversion assertions are based only on the speaker's personal experience, without methodology or sample details.
The excerpt explicitly recommends auto-sorting landing-page reviews based on included images and videos and states that media reviews are more valuable than text-only reviews.
The candidate does not add unspecified ranking mechanics or platform-specific implementation claims.

The excerpt supports the examples of a $10 next-order gift card and a $10 refund for a review with an image, as well as the distinction the speaker makes between incentivizing reviews and directly paying for reviews.

The action lacks the source's material condition that image/video-review incentives be legal and compliant in the country being advertised in; this should be an explicit prerequisite or limitation rather than only an unknown.

The dependency on candidate 34c1… is backwards or at least unsupported as a strict prerequisite: incentivizing people to submit reviews is presented as a way to obtain reviews, not as something requiring prior completion of review collection.
The excerpt expressly says that proof matters only when it matches the claim and gives custom landing pages for personas and concepts as the reason to tailor proof.
The candidate accurately preserves the limitation that generic positive reviews do not substantiate a specific claimed outcome.

The candidate accurately reports the source's stated lesson from the worked offer: positioning the three products as steps toward an outcome, rather than relying on price, is what the speaker says was done well.
It appropriately identifies this as a qualitative source assertion rather than a controlled comparison.

source_limitations: The excerpt begins mid-thought and ends mid-sentence, so adjacent context is unavailable, particularly for the final proof example.
Many performance assertions are attributed only to the speaker's own e-commerce stores in 2019–2020; no samples, product categories, traffic volumes, controls, or measurement methods are supplied.

The $122 routine, $14 shipping/fulfillment saving, $60 gift threshold, $66 shipping threshold, and $19 post-checkout upsell are presented within a skincare worked example, not as validated general thresholds.
The legal statements about paid or incentivized reviews are jurisdictionally vague and provide no governing law, compliance requirements, or disclosure rules.
No platform, payment processor, or implementation details are supplied to establish that one-click cart upgrades, review sorting, or repeat card billing work universally.

source.text: allows you to have higher conversion rates and higher average order value. Uh, bundles work really well because they allow you to pass on the shipping and fulfillment efficiency to the customer while pushing up units per transaction, which is one of the biggest levers that underpins average order value. And then there's two additional levers that no one really talks about properly, which is shipping. Free shipping is not always the win that it looks like because it teaches the customer to value delivery separately from the product. And shipping collected is almost pure profit for most people. Most people can charge shipping up to about 10% of the average order value of the cart. And it won't impact conversion rate at all. And I ran a lot of tests myself on my own e-commerce stores back in 2019 2020 on this. I did a lot of free shipping testing, introducing shipping back in, putting shipping insurance, putting expedited shipping, all of these different options. And generally speaking, as long as you keep your shipping collected at sub 10% of total revenue, it has no material impact on conversion rates. And so if you're going to give away free shipping, you definitely want to give it away at a threshold to incentivize people up. And then if you're going to do it at a threshold, you want to be very specific as to where you place that threshold and do a lot of testing around it because most people set their free shipping threshold way too low. Now the second lever that exists is the post-purchase upsell. Right after they buy, one click, no re-entering their card. You can just bill them a second time with a oneclick upsell. It obviously has to be relevant to what they just bought, not a random add-on, but it's the cleanest, easiest way to increase average order value because you're presenting it right as they're the warmest within the entire funnel because they've just spent money and you hit them with obviously a discount on that cross-eller upsell. Ends up having a very high take rate, increases revenue per visitor. So now going back to our example, we have a bad offer on the left, a good offer on the right, honing in on the left, we've got a 20% off. Obviously, this is going to erode margin enormously. It's just lazy discounting. It's not increasing average order value. This is what most people do. Revenue is going to go up, sure, but profit is going to go down here. Now, this is also going to train the customer to wait for discounts. People that start doing 20% off everything discounts pretty quickly. Everyone knows them for doing 20% off everything discounts and they can't get out of this rut and so they become reliant on it. Now, we have a good offer on the right. There's a lot going on here, but this is what the best direct to consumer brands are doing at the moment. So, we've moved away from the overnight repair serum, and we've moved into a routine bundle. The bundle has a gentle cleanser, overnight repair serum, and then the recovery night cream. And each of these is framed as a different step. And so, you need each of these steps to actually be able to achieve the outcome that you're after. Immediately by doing this, it's increased our average order value to $122. Now, what we've also done is we've baked in a discount across the bundle. Now, the discount that we're giving is $14. So, normally this is valued at $136, but we're going to give it for $122. We lose no margin here because we are just passing on our economies of scale from shipping these three items together. If we were to ship them separately, we would have to pay shipping and fulfillment costs three separate times, which would have cost us an additional $14. But shipping them together, we save on the duplication of shipping fees. Therefore, our margin is the same. We don't actually lose any margin giving this discount away. We're just passing on our shipping and fulfillment savings. Now, in addition to putting a bundle together here, which is maintaining margin and improving average order value. On top of that, we have two things up the top. Number one, we have a free travel size ritual set, which is worth $30. Now, it's priced at $30. Cost of goods to us might just be $4 or $5. It's going to be very low. We always want to put a gift that's very low cost, but high perceived value. And that's added to all orders over $60. So, right away, this is our first incentive at the $60 mark. If someone went and bought this on the left, they wouldn't get the gift. But if they go and buy the full routine, which is a much better option because it will actually allow them to achieve their outcome, we will also then throw in a free gift. We're also going to give away free shipping at 66. Now, this would need to be really thoughtful as to do we really want it at 66, do we want it a little bit higher? We'd obviously need to dial this in, test it over time, but we've got a free shipping offer there. But then really the key of this whole landing page is that yes, we can drive traffic straight to the routine page, but we can continue driving traffic to just the overnight repair serum. When people click add to cart, this is what appears in the cart. They haven't achieved free [snorts] shipping yet. They're not getting their free travel gift, but the way that they can get a free travel gift and they can get free shipping and they can save money is by adding the routine to cart. So, this is a one-click upgrade of the cart which upgrades them from just buying the overnight serum to adding in the cleanser and the recovery night cream. It is such a good frame of here is the enormous amount of free stuff that we're going to give you and you're going to save so much money by adding this stuff into cart and tripling your average order value for a brand like this. This change alone just to the cart slide out is going to make an enormous difference in revenue per visitor. Now, on top of this, after checkout, we're going to add a uh postcheckout oneclick upsell, which is going to be the ritual bag for $19. Now, we're going to obviously frame this as it's typically at 35 or $40 and it's discounted for 50% for 5 minutes post checkout. And so, this is also going to further increase our revenue per visitor on this pack. So, what's done well here, the offer is positioning. It's not discounting. Once again, we are not losing any margin here. The free shipping we're happy to give away because the average order value is high enough that the cost of shipping has democratized. We're happy to give away the $14 here because we're actually saving on shipping and fulfillment cost by shipping this all together. The free gift is $4 and so the margin impact is very minimal. And so this all came down to positioning as these three steps are your solution to be able to actually get your outcome than it was to do with price. The gift with purchase improves break even rorowaz. The bundle lifts units per transaction. And then we have a threshold and an upsell which is both going to increase revenue per visitor. Moving into the next element, which is proof. Number one, most obvious one with proof is reviews. If you have no reviews, nothing else in this chapter really matters because getting from zero reviews to 100 reviews can roughly double your conversion rate. And I say that from personal experience running my own multiple e-commerce brands during 2019 to 2020. I found that one of the easiest ways to just double conversion rates overnight was to go from not having reviews to having reviews. It's one of the biggest trust signal that exists. I imagine 99% of people watching this have it already, so I don't need to spend much time on it. But if you're a startup and you're wondering, do I really need to worry about reviews at this stage? The answer is absolutely yes. It's the biggest trust signal. Worth noting that really it's from 0 to 80 reviews where the big conversion rate jump comes from. After that, it's really kind of immeasurable. You can go from 80 to 150 to 300 to 400. It's it's all really the same. It's not going to change in the consumer's eyes. Uh a little hack that you want to do here with reviews is you want them auto sorting on the landing page uh based on images and videos that are dropped within them. Images and videos are way more valuable of a review than just a text review. In fact, I would honestly want to incentivize towards image and videos as long as it's legal and compliant in the country that you're advertising in. You can't technically pay people in most countries for to give you a review. That's illegal. But you can incentivize people towards giving a review. And so you can say something like $10 gift card on your next order for a review. Or what some people do, which I really like is a cash back. And so uh if you drop us a review with an image, we will refund $10 off your order. And so you just get the cash straight back from the order. Um, I would definitely employ strategies like that if you're a newer brand and you need to try to maximize as many reviews as possible and you want to get a bunch of images and videos on the landing page, too. Uh, number two is that proof doesn't matter unless it matches the claim that you're making. And so, this is why custom landing pages for different personas and concepts is actually really important because you can go and reinforce a bunch of proof, but if it's on something that the customer doesn't care about or it's super generic, then it is actually meaningless and the proof doesn't matter. For example, if we're pushing people to the landing page so they can have firmer skin within 4 weeks and then the landing page just has a bunch of reviews on it or a bunch of social proof testimonials, whatever it might be, just saying the product is great.
